title: Mohit Kumar vs Hemlata on 22 June, 2024
full_text: Mohit Kumar vs Hemlata on 22 June, 2024 IN THE COURT OF MS. NEHA GARG, METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE (N.I. ACT)- 02, PATIALA HOUSE DISTRICT COURT: NEW DELHI DLND020182772020 Case No: 10357/2020 Mohit Kumar s/o Sh. Rajender Kumar r/o 10756, Subhash Park, Gali no.2, Naveen Shahdara, Delhi - 110032. ...... Complainant ::Versus:: Smt. Hemlata w/o Sh. Parveen Kumar, r/o J-77A, Block-J, Mohan Garden, Uttam Nagar, Delhi - 110059 And Also at H.No.3739, Churi Walan, Chawari Bazar, Delhi - 110006 .......Accused Offence Complained of: 138 of the NI Act Plea of the Accused: Not guilty Date of Institution: 09.11.2020 Arguments Heard On: 21.05.2024 Date of Judgment: 22.06.2024 Decision: CONVICTION JUDGMENT 1. Vide this judgment, I shall decide the present complaint Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA GARG Mohit Kumar vs. Hemlata GARG Date: 2024.06.22 Case no.10357/2020 Page 1 of 16 22:58:28 +0530 filed u/s 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (herein after referred to as 'the NI Act ') bearing CC No.10357/2020, against the dishonor of cheque bearing no.929985 dated 20.09.2020 for a sum of Rs.2,14,000/- drawn on Syndicate Bank, Civic Centre, Minto Road, New Delhi (hereinafter referred to as 'the cheque in question'). 2. Shorn to unnecessary details, the brief facts of the case put forth by the complainant are that the complainant are having friendship relation with the husband of accused for the last about 10 years and accordingly the accused requested the complainant to arrange some money for the accused for some personal requirement and the complainant advanced the accused a friendly loan of Rs.2,14,000/- on 25.08.2018 in the presence of one Sh. Johnee Bharti. It is further stated that accused promised to return the said loan amount within a period of two years along with interest @24% per annum. However, on repeated request and demands of complainant, accused issued the cheque in question towards the discharge of her liability. It is further state that the accused had given writing in favour of complainant and the same is duly signed by the accused and her mother-in-law namely Smt. Shakuntala and Sister-in-law (nanad) Smt. Jyoti at the time of issuance of the cheque in question. 3. The accused had assured the complainant the said cheque would be honoured on presentation, however, the same was dishonored with the remarks 'funds insufficient' vide cheque returning memo. Legal demand notice dated 03.10.2020 was sent to the accused. However, no payment was made within 15 days Digitally signed by NEHA Mohit Kumar vs. Hemlata NEHA GARG Case no.10357/2020 Page 2 of 16 GARG Date: 2024.06.22 22:58:44 +0530 and hence, the present complaint. 4. The complainant examined himself as CW-1 in pre- summoning evidence, and relied upon his evidence by way of affidavit along with the following documents: - S.No Documents relied upon Exhibited as: 1. Cheque in question Ex.CW-1/1 2. Hand written undertaking Ex.CW-1/2 given by the accused. 3. Bank return memo. Ex.CW-1/3 4. Legal demand notice. Ex.CW-1/4 5. Speed Postal receipts. Ex.CW-1/5 & Ex.CW-1/6 6. Internet tracking report. Ex.CW-1/7 & Ex.CW-1/8 5. On appearance of accused, notice of accusation u/s 251 of Cr.P.C was served upon the accused to which the accused pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. Accused admitted her signature on the cheque in question and stated that she has filled the particulars of the cheque under pressure from the complainant. She stated that she has not received the legal demand notice from the complainant, however, she stated that the address of 'Uttam Nagar' mentioned on the legal demand notice is hers. She further stated that she had taken Rs.1,40,000/- from the complainant in cash and she had already repaid Rs.80,000/- by bank account transfer. She further stated that the remaining amount of Rs.60,000/- has been transferred in the account of one Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA GARG Mohit Kumar vs. Hemlata GARG Date: 2024.06.22 22:59:07 Case no.10357/2020 Page 3 of 16 +0530 person named Johny Bharti at the insistence of the complainant. She stated that she has no liability towards the complainant and her cheque has been misused. 6. Thereafter, an oral application u/s 145(2) of the NI Act was moved on behalf of accused which was allowed by the court. Thereafter matter was listed for CE. Thereafter, CW1 was examined in chief, cross-examined and discharged. Complainant also examined witness from post office namely Sh. Nazir as CW5. Thereafter, CE was closed. Thereafter, all the incriminating evidence was put to the accused and the statement u/s 313 of Cr.P.C. of accused was recorded in which accused reiterated her defence. Accused chose to lead DE and thereafter matter was listed for defence evidence. 7. Perusal of the record shows that subsequently the accused chose not to lead DE and separate statement of accused was recorded to the aforesaid effect. Further, accused also arrived at settlement with the accused but she did not make any payment. Thereafter matter was listed for final arguments. 8. Final arguments have been heard on behalf of the complainant; however, no final arguments have been addressed on behalf of accused despite opportunity. I have considered the evidence led by both the sides carefully and have perused the Court records thoroughly. INGREDIENTS OF OFFENCE UNDER CONSIDERATION: 9. Before going into the facts of the present case, it would be apposite to discuss the legal standards required to be met by both Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA GARG Mohit Kumar vs. Hemlata GARG Date: 2024.06.22 Case no.10357/2020 Page 4 of 16 22:59:18 +0530 sides. In order to establish the offence under Section 138 of the NI Act, the prosecution must fulfill all the essential ingredients of the offence, as highlighted below: 1st Ingredient: The cheque was drawn by a person on an account maintained by him/her for payment of money and the same is presented for payment within a period of 3 months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity; 2nd Ingredient: The cheque was drawn by the drawer for discharge of any legally enforceable debt or other liability; 3rd Ingredient: The cheque was returned unpaid by the bank due to either insufficiency of funds in the account to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account on an agreement made with that bank; 4th Ingredient: A demand of the said amount has been made by the payee or holder in due course of the cheque by a notice in writing given to the drawer within thirty days of the receipt of information of the dishonour of cheque from the bank; 5th Ingredient: The drawer fails to make payment of the said amount of money within fifteen days from the date of receipt of notice. 10. Once the ingredients mentioned in the foregoing paragraph are established by the complainant, then as soon as the execution of the impugned cheque is admitted by the accused, a factual base is established to invoke the presumption of cheque having been issued in discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other Digitally signed by Mohit Kumar vs. Hemlata NEHA NEHA Date : GARG GARG 2024.06.22 Case no.10357/2020 Page 5 of 16 22:59:28 +0530 liability by virtue of Section 118(a) read with Section 139 of the NI Act. This is a reverse onus clause, which means that unless the contrary is proved, it shall be presumed that the impugned cheque was drawn by the accused for a consideration and that the complainant had received it in discharge of a debt/ liability from the accused. In the case titled as Bir Singh vs. Mukesh Kumar , (2019) 4 SCC 197, it was held by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India that once the accused has admitted the signatures on the impugned cheque, then the court is bound to raise presumption under Section 139 of the NI Act. 11. It has been held by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the judgment titled Rangappa vs. Sri Mohan , (2010) 11 SCC 441 that a reverse onus clause usually imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden and when an accused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139 of the NI Act, the standard of proof for doing so is that of "preponderance of probabilities". Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prosecution can fail. It was further held that the accused can rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise such a defence and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not need to adduce evidence of his own. 12. Ld. Counsel for the complainant has submitted that accused should be convicted of offence u/s 138 of the NI Act because the complainant has proved the original cheque, which the accused has not disputed as being drawn on the account of Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA GARG Mohit Kumar vs. Hemlata GARG Date: Case no.10357/2020 Page 6 of 16 2024.06.22 22:59:43 +0530 the accused. He has further submitted the cheque in question was returned unpaid vide cheque return memo which is on record. The same is also not disputed by accused. He has further submitted that the legal demand notice was sent to accused on the admitted 'Uttam Nagar' address of the accused and the same is proved by postal receipt. He has further submitted that the fact that the payment was not made within 15 days of the receipt of the legal notice is also not disputed. 13. Before examining the defences of accused, it is pertinent to note that the accused has admitted her signatures on the cheque in question. Accordingly, this Court raises presumption under Section 118(a) and 139 of the NI Act that the cheque in question was issued by the accused to the complainant in discharge of legally enforceable debt or liability. In order to rebut the presumptions, the burden of proof shifts to the accused to prove on a preponderance of probabilities that there was no liability for the amount of the cheque in question. Therefore, in the present matter, the onus of proof is now upon the accused to raise a probable defence and to rebut the presumption of the existence of a legally recoverable debt arisen in favour of the complainant. Now I shall be discussing all the defences of the accused one by one. 14. In order to assess the 'probable defence', if any, raised by the accused, it is pertinent to evaluate and appreciate the plea of defence of accused recorded u/s 251 of Cr.P.C., statement of accused recorded u/s 313 of Cr.P.C. as well as the suggestions Digitally put to the complainant in his cross-examination. signed by NEHA NEHA GARG GARG Date: 2024.06.22 Mohit Kumar vs. Hemlata 22:59:54 +0530 Case no.10357/2020 Page 7 of 16 DEFENCES OF THE ACCUSED: I. Defence that legal demand notice was not received: 15. It is the defense of the accused that she didn't receive the legal demand notice. It is pertinent to mention that the accused has admitted that the address of 'Uttam Nagar' mentioned on the legal demand notice is hers. Furthermore, the address of 'Chawri Bazar' as mentioned in the legal demand notice is the one as provided in the pronote Ex.CW1/2, execution of which is not denied by the accused. Complainant has placed on record the original postal receipts to prove the service of legal demand notice upon the admitted addresses of accused. 16. It is worthwhile to note that Section 27 of General Clauses Act, 1897 deals with the presumption of service of notice sent by post and provides that service of such notice shall be deemed to have been affected unless the contrary is proved. At this stage it is apposite to discuss the judgment of the Division Bench of the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Prakash Jewellers vs A.K. Jewellers , 99 (2002) DLT 244 wherein also, the accused had taken the defence that he had not received the notice under Section 138 of the NI Act. The Hon'ble High Court dismissed the objections and held as under: "8. There is no dispute with the proposition that a statutory obligation is cast on the holder of the cheque or the payee to give notice of demand to the drawer of the cheque asking him to make a payment of the amount covered by the cheque. It is a mandatory requirement to be satisfied for constituting an offence under Section 138 . Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA GARG GARG Date: 2024.06.22 Mohit Kumar vs. Hemlata 23:00:01 +0530 Case no.10357/2020 Page 8 of 16 9. It is also settled that it is not the giving of the notice which makes out an offence but its receipt which furnishes a cause of action to the complainant to file the complaint within statutory period. 10. As it is, Section 138 does not prescribe any mode for giving of demand notice by the payee or holder of the cheque. But where such notice is served by post through registered post or postal certificate, etc. with the correct address of the drawer written on it, it would raise a presumption of service unless the drawer proves that it was not received by him in fact and that he was not responsible for such non-service. This is in tune with the principle embodied in Section 27 of the General Clauses Act or even Rule 19-A of Order V CPC . 11. Section 27of General Clauses Act deals with the presumption of service of notice sent by post and provides that service of such notice shall be deemed to have been affected unless the contrary is proved. This principle is equally applicable to the service of notice for purpose of Section 138 of Negotiable Instrument Act also...... 12. Proceeding on this premise and going by this logic, we find no hitch in taking the view that payee or the holder of a cheque was as much entitled to claim the benefit of presumption of service once he had dispatched the demand notice through registered post or postal certificate on the correct address of the sendee written on it and where he had proved such dispatch through original receipts. It becomes inconsequential whether sender had not received back the AD card or that he could Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA GARG GARG Date: 2024.06.22 Mohit Kumar vs. Hemlata 23:00:07 +0530 Case no.10357/2020 Page 9 of 16 not produce or prove it for having misplaced it or for some other reason." (Emphasis supplied) 17. In the present case also, complainant has proved that he had issued a legal notice under Section 138 of the NI Act and the same is duly proved by the original postal receipts placed on record by the complainant. In any case, the service of legal notice is to be presumed in view of the afore cited judgment of the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi. 18. Moreover, it was held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the decision cited as C.C. Alavi Haji vs Palapetty Muhammed &Anr. (2007) 6 SCC 555 that a person who does not pay within 15 days of receipt of the summons from the Court along with the copy of the complaint under Section 138 of the Act, cannot obvi- ously contend that there was no proper service of notice as re- quired under Section 138 , by ignoring statutory presumption to the contrary under Section 27 of the General Clauses Act and Section 114 of the Evidence Act. 19. The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India has very well dis- cussed this defence in K. Bhaskaran vs Sankaran Vaidhyan Balan and Anr. (1999) 7 SCC 510, where it was held that if a strict in- terpretation is given that the drawer should have actually re- ceived the notice for the period of 15 days to start running no matter that the payee sent the notice on the correct address, a trickster cheque drawer would get the premium to avoid receiv- ing the notice by different strategies and he could escape from the legal consequences of Section 138 of the NI Act. Thus, for Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA GARG GARG Date: Mohit Kumar vs. Hemlata 2024.06.22 23:00:15 Case no.10357/2020 Page 10 of 16 +0530 the detailed reasons aforementioned, the plea of the accused that the legal demand notice was never received is not tenable and the same accordingly stands rejected. II. Defence that there is no legally enforceable debt or liability: 20. From the perusal of the notice u/s 251 Cr.P.C as well as statement of accused u/s 313 Cr.P.C, it is clear that it is the defence of accused that she had taken cash loan of Rs.1,40,000/- from the complainant out of which she is stated to have repaid Rs.80,000/- through bank transfer and the reaming amount of Rs.60,000/- is stated to have been transferred in the account of Johny Bharti at the insistence of the complainant. 21. It is worthwhile to mention here that the accused can prove her defence by drawing inferences from the materials already on record (including complainant's evidences), circumstances of the case and also leading her own evidence. As stated earlier, the accused has not led any defense evidence in support of her case. Therefore, the case set up by the accused needs to be drawn from the suggestions put to the complainant during his cross- examination. 22. It has been suggested to the complainant in his cross- examination that no loan of Rs.2,14,000/- was given to the accused but rather a sum of Rs.1,40,000/- was advanced to the accused. It has further been suggested to the compliant that the amount of Rs.1,40,000/- was advanced without any interest and the amount of Rs.60,000/- was transferred by the accused to the Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA GARG Mohit Kumar vs. Hemlata GARG Date: 2024.06.22 23:00:22 Case no.10357/2020 Page 11 of 16 +0530 Mr. Johny Bharti by cash and bank account transfer on the instructions of the complainant. It has been suggested to the complainant that the cheque in question was obtained by creating pressure on the accused by the complainant alongwith 4-5 persons. It has been further suggested to the complainant that pronote Ex.CW1/2 has been executed and obtained by exerting pressure/threat on the accused. It is pertinent to note here that all the aforesaid suggestions have been denied by the complainant. 23. Apart from the aforesaid suggestions put to the complainant in his cross-examination, the accused has not brought any substantive evidence in support of the defence set up by her. Complainant has deposed in his examination-in-chief that the impugned loan amount was advanced to the accused in the presence of Johny Bharti. Complainant has not been cross- examined on his aforesaid statement and therefore, the testimony of the complainant that Johny Bharti was present when the loan amount was advanced to the accused has gone unrebutted. However, the accused made no efforts to examine Johny Bharti to prove that she has actually borrowed Rs.1,40,000/- from the complainant and not a sum of Rs.2,41,000/- despite the fact that husband of the accused knows Johny Bharti as is evident from the suggestion put to the complainant during his cross- examination. The non-examination of Johny Bharti by the accused in support of her defence is a material omission on the part of the accused. 24. It has been suggested to the complainant in his cross- examination that pronote Ex.CW1/2 has been executed and Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA GARG GARG Date: 2024.06.22 Mohit Kumar vs. Hemlata 23:00:28 +0530 Case no.10357/2020 Page 12 of 16 obtained by exerting pressure/threat on the accused. In other words, accused has not denied the execution of the pronote but it is the defence of the accused that she was pressurized/threatened to execute the same. The aforesaid defence of the accused appears to be bald assertions uncorroborated by any evidence as the circumstances surrounding the alleged pressurization/threat have not been explained by the accused. Pronote Ex.CW1/2 is signed by two witnesses, which the complainant has deposed are the mother-in-law and Sister-in-law (nanad) of the accused. However, the accused has not examined her aforesaid two family members in support of her aforesaid defence. Therefore, this Court is of the view that the accused has been unable to prove that she was pressurized/threatened to execute the pronote. Pronote Ex.CW1/2 is a clinching piece of evidence fastening liability on the accused to the tune of the amount of the cheque in question. 25. Accused has also tried to challenge the source of funds of the complainant by suggesting to the complainant in his cross- examination that the impugned loan amount was not arranged by selling any property as asserted by the complainant. In the considered opinion of this Court, the cross-examination of the complainant to the aforesaid effect is insignificant as admittedly the accused has obtained a sum of Rs.1,40,000/- from the complainant. If the complainant had the funds to advance a sum of Rs.1,40,000/- in cash to the accused, he surely has the financial capacity and the funds to advance a sum of Rs.2,14,000/- to the accused. Therefore, this Court is of the view that by admitting that she has borrowed a sum of Rs.1,40,000/- Digitally signed by NEHA Mohit Kumar vs. Hemlata NEHA GARG Case no.10357/2020 Page 13 of 16 GARG Date: 2024.06.22 23:00:34 +0530 from the complainant, the accused has lent credence to the financial capacity and source of funds of the complainant to advance the impugned loan amount. 26. Complainant has also been cross-examined to the effect that he has not mentioned the loan amount in his ITR. However, the fact the complainant has not shown the alleged loan amount in his ITR cannot be the sole reason to doubt the case of the prosecution as the accused admits having taken a loan of Rs.1,40,000/- from the complainant. Moreover, the culpability of offence under Section 138 of the NI Act will not freeze for the reason that there is violation of Section 269 of Income Tax Act, 1961 and the same does not prevent the operation of the statutory presumption of section 139 of the NI Act. A bare reading of the provision enshrined in section 269SS of the of the Income Tax Act, 1961 would suggest that the said provision only regulates the mode of accepting deposits or loans. It does not per se declare all transactions in cash above the threshold of Rs. 20,000/- illegal. Accordingly, prosecution u/S. 138 of the NI Act cannot be dismissed or stalled for non-compliance of Section 269 SS of the Income Tax Act. 27. It is also the defence of the accused that she has transferred an amount of Rs.60,000/- to Johny Bharti through cash and bank transfer at the behest of the compliant. The accused has neither examined Johny Bharti in support of her aforesaid defence and nor has she placed on record her bank account statement to evidence the payments, if any, made to the said person. Therefore, the defence of the accused that she has made payment Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA GARG Mohit Kumar vs. Hemlata GARG Date: 2024.06.22 23:00:40 Case no.10357/2020 Page 14 of 16 +0530 of Rs.60,000/- to Johny Bharti also appears only to be bald assertions unsupported by any evidence. Complainant has not denied that he has received a part payment of Rs.80,000/- from the accused, however, complainant has deposed that the aforesaid amount was received only after the service of the legal demand notice. It is also a matter of record that the accused has made a payment of Rs.18,000/- during the pendency of the trial. The aforesaid part payments made by the accused can be considered at the time of sentencing, however, the same does not absolve the accused of his criminal liability. 28. A meticulous perusal of the cross-examination of the complainant reveals that nothing significant has been brought in the cross-examination of the complainant to raise any suspicion in the case set up by the complainant. The case of the complainant has been consistent throughout as can be noticed from a perusal of the complaint, demand notice and affidavit evidence. Mere suggestions put to the complainant in his cross- examination will not take place of substantive prof and the same will not help the accused to discharge the burden of proof cast on her to prove on a preponderance of probabilities that there was no liability for the amount of the cheque in question. 29. It is also worthwhile to note that the accused had settled the matter with the complainant in Court on 11.08.2023 and despite the aforesaid settlement, she failed to make the payment. 30. Since the accused has not disputed the signatures of the cheque in question, the presumption under Sections 118 and 139 Digitally signed by NEHA NEHA GARG GARG Date: Mohit Kumar vs. Hemlata 2024.06.22 23:00:46 Case no.10357/2020 Page 15 of 16 +0530 of the NI Act takes effect and the complainant's case satisfies all the ingredients necessary for securing a conviction under Section 138 of the NI Act. The defense of the accused was that the cheque in question was not issued in discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability. The accused having miserably failed to discharge her evidential burden, that fact will have to be taken to be proved by force of the presumption, without requiring anything more from the complainant. Accordingly, the defence of the accused that there is no legally enforceable debt or liability of the accused towards the complainant for cheque amount in question goes unproved and the same accordingly stands rejected. FINAL ORDER: 31. On a consideration of the totality of factors pleaded by the accused in his defence, it becomes clear that the accused has merely paid lip service to his defence and has not led any cogent evidence to establish it or draw any circumstance against the case of the complainant which probabilizes his defence. 32. Accordingly, the accused Hemlata w/o Sh. Parveen Kumar is convicted of the offence u/s. 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. Announced in open Court Note: This judgment contains 16 pages and each page has been Digitally signed by signed by me.
